in_text_mentions: In 2012, a 44-year-old female, with a family history of unspecified cerebral tumors, was brought to the outpatient clinic due to cephalea and right-sided gait lateropulsion, which she had experienced for the last seven years. A CT scan revealed hydrocephalus. Thus, a ventriculoperitoneal shunt was placed. In September 2013, she started experiencing cephalea and dizziness. MRI displayed a left cerebellar hemispheric lesion with a “tiger stripe” appearance (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 7 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F, G). A: H&E histology from a confirmed Lhermitte-Duclos disease case showing large dysplastic ganglion cells, a classic histologic manifestation. B: H&E histology from a confirmed Lhermitte-Duclos disease case showing dysplastic ganglion cells infiltrating cerebellar cortex. C: H&E histology from a confirmed Lhermitte-Duclos disease case showing dysplastic ganglion cells with fine chromatin, prominent nucleolus, and hemorrhage. D: Immunohistochemistry from a confirmed Lhermitte-Duclos disease case showing NSE-positive dysplastic ganglion cells. E: Immunohistochemistry from a confirmed Lhermitte-Duclos disease case showing synaptophysin-positive dysplastic ganglion cells. F: Immunohistochemistry from a confirmed Lhermitte-Duclos disease case showing ganglion cells with normal neurofilament configuration. G: Immunohistochemistry from a confirmed Lhermitte-Duclos disease case showing GFAP-reactive astrocytes surrounding ganglion cells.

in_text_mentions: A CT scan of her brain, performed before a cerebral PET scan, showed a hypodense mass in her left cerebellar hemisphere. Brain PET revealed intense and focal uptake of the tracer in the left hemisphere of her cerebellum, corresponding to the lesion discovered by CT, with an SUVmax of 14, while the SUVmax in the contralateral cerebellar hemisphere was 6.5 (Figure 1a).

ondition. Four days later, MRI of her brain was performed. This revealed a slightly-enhancing, bulky mass in her right cerebellar hemisphere that measured 5 × 4 × 3 cm. On T1-weighted images, the lesion was hypointense and slightly enhancing after the administration of gadolinium. The T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) images showed the characteristic features of LDD: striations representing the folia of the cerebellum in association with hydrocephalus and dislocation of the fourth ventricle (Figure 1b,c). MRI was performed using a 3-T permanent magnet (GE Medical System).

Image analysis of PET/MRI-fused images was performed by a nuclear medicine physician and a radiologist. The borders of the lesion were correctly fused and integrated PET/MRI views confirmed our suspicion that F18-FDG was taken up heterogeneously within the tumor, similarly to isointense bands of tissue in corresponding T2-weighted FLAIR images. Furthermore, by analysis of the PET/MRI images, we had confirmation of a lesion with similar metabolism and intensity signal to normal grey matter; the PET-only brain images suggested a hypothesis of a malignant neoplasm (Figure 1d).

round or round-like space-occupying lesions involving one or both cerebellar hemispheres

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Axial T2 MRI of a 40-year-old female with Lhermitte-Duclos disease shows the classic tiger-striped cerebellar lesion; article and caption support LDD. B: Axial T1 MRI of the same LDD patient shows the tiger-striped cerebellar lesion, a classic imaging feature. C: Axial MRI of the LDD patient with captioned limited diffusion in the cerebellar lesion; finding is not represented in the provided vocabulary, so it is proposed. D: Axial enhanced MRI of the LDD patient showing vascular-like enhancement in the cerebellar lesion; enhancement is not typical for LDD and not in the provided vocabulary.

in_text_mentions: In previous pathological reports, MRI mostly showed round or round-like space-occupying lesions involving one or both cerebellar hemispheres (all 3 patients in our center were affected unilaterally).[12,13] Although the degree of malignancy of this disease is not high, it usually involves a wide range of conditions, which can cause displacement of the fourth ventricle and obstructive hydrocephalus. In almost all cases, conventional MRI can clearly show the “tiger striped” sign of an LDD. The pathology in our center is consistent with that in previous reports (Fig. 2).[14]

panels.figure_caption: Pre-operative brain MRI of an eight-year-old boy with Lhermitte-Duclos disease (LDD) (a) Axial T2-weighted image showing patchy high-signal lesion in the left cerebellum with mass effect and compression of the fourth ventricle. The classic tiger-stripe appearance is considered typical for LDD; (b) Coronal T1-weighted image showing low-signal lesion in the left cerebellum (typical finding); (c) Axial diffusion weighted imaging (DWI) showing high signal (restricted diffusion); (d–f) Axial, coronal, and sagittal contrasted T1-weighted images.
in_text_mentions: nced cranial MRI was performed done and showed an ill-defined left-cerebellar lesion with patchy high signals both in T2 and flair imaging and low signals in T1 imaging with restriction in diffusion weighted imaging (DWI). No definite mass noted with contrast enhancement following sulci distribution (see Figure 2). Furthermore, the DWI sequence did not show any diffusion restriction. The potential differential diagnoses were LDD, viral infection, acute ischemic insult, and leukemia. In the next four days, the patient did fine with no complaints and was prepared for partial resection operation.

plate_findings.evidence: Cerebellar cortex replaced by tumor (H&E; 4x) — visual
Dysplastic ganglion cells infiltrating the molecular layer

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Patient histology from a case series of Lhermitte-Duclos disease showing tumor replacement of cerebellar cortex; confirmed dysplastic gangliocytoma in the text. B: Kluver-Barrera stain demonstrating dysplastic ganglion cells in the molecular layer, a hallmark histologic feature of Lhermitte-Duclos disease. C: High-power H&E showing dysplastic ganglion cells with vacuolated stroma, characteristic of Lhermitte-Duclos disease. D: NeuN immunostain confirming neuronal (ganglion cell) phenotype of the dysplastic cells in Lhermitte-Duclos disease. E: GFAP stain showing reactive astrocytes surrounding the dysplastic ganglion cells of the patient's cerebellar dysplastic gangliocytoma. F: Neuron-specific enolase immunostain confirming ganglion cell differentiation in the dysplastic cerebellar gangliocytoma.

in_text_mentions: The surgical specimen was reported as a pale grayish soft tumor with irregular thickening of the left cerebellar folia (Figure 3A). The histopathology report described a replacement of the granular layer by dysplastic ganglion cells, attenuated Purkinje cell layer, and subpial neurons in the molecular layer confirmed with immunohistochemistry positive for NeuN and synaptophysin, which are characteristic findings of cerebellar dysplastic gangliocytoma or LDD (Figures 3B-3G).

on with deep extension [1,2]. The characteristic histopathological findings of LDD are a relative conservation of the cerebellar architecture with folia thickness as a consequence of a diffuse granular and molecular layer, which usually contains ganglion cells of multiple sizes, morphologically dispersed cells, and an attenuated or absent Purkinje cell layer. In the present case, abundant ganglion cells were reported in the granular layer, in which the Purkinje cells were partially conserved, and there was a conserved molecular layer with small groups of subpial ganglion cells (Figures 3B-3G).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Panel A shows the sagittal T1-WI of a left upper cerebellar hemisphere lesion, consistent with Lhermitte-Duclos disease as described in the caption. B: Panel B demonstrates the coronal T2-WI, showing the lesion with a characteristic striated appearance, supporting Lhermitte-Duclos disease. C: Panel C is a sagittal post-contrast T1-WI showing the lesion does not enhance after gadolinium injection, consistent with the description of LD. D: Panel D shows Diffusion WI, demonstrating high intensity in the lesion, as noted in the caption. E: Panel E displays the FLAIR sequence, showing high intensity of the cerebellar lesion, consistent with Lhermitte-Duclos disease. F: Panel F displays an MRS spectrum showing a moderately decreased choline/Creatine ratio, a characteristic finding for the lesion.
